target.title: fix(slack): suppress progress chrome sends
target.body:
## Summary
- detect progress-only Slack tool chrome payloads with leading tool emoji plus command/status body
- convert thread-scoped chrome to reactions instead of `chat.postMessage`
- fail closed by suppressing chrome without a reaction target while preserving semantic replies
- type automatic tool-progress payloads at the producer boundary with a closed generic plugin-SDK progress intent so Slack does not infer from arbitrary text

## What Problem This Solves
Progress-only operational chrome like `:hammer_and_wrench: \`pnpm test\`` or `:writing_hand: Write: MEMORY.md` can leak into Slack as user-visible messages when a tool/status payload accidentally reaches the Slack send path. This creates noise in working channels and violates the progress-chrome pre-send gate. The Slack extension now classifies only narrow progress-only payloads and prevents them from becoming chat posts.

## Evidence
Current head: `1e3f34f78d97ec5790a39b722f55b53e640488c5`.

- `pnpm --config.verify-deps-before-run=false vitest run --project extension-codex extensions/codex/src/app-server/event-projector.test.ts` passed (149 tests)
- focused Slack replies + identity-fallback tests passed (85 tests)
- `test/scripts/plugin-sdk-surface-report.test.ts` passed (10 tests)
- `pnpm --config.verify-deps-before-run=false tsgo:extensions` passed
- formatter check on touched files passed
- `git diff --check` passed

## Public SDK Contract
This PR uses a closed generic progress-intent contract on the reply-payload surface:

- shared field: `channelData.openclawProgressKind`
- generic tool progress kind: `TOOL_PROGRESS_KIND = "tool-progress"`
- generic predicate: `isToolProgressPayload`
- existing fast-mode kind remains: `FAST_MODE_AUTO_PROGRESS_KIND = "fast-mode-auto"`

Codex no longer exports Codex-named public progress symbols. Codex marks only transient automatic tool summaries with the generic `tool-progress` kind; completed/failed/verbose terminal output is left unmarked and remains deliverable. Callable public SDK budget was raised with the additive predicate.

target.title: fix(sessions): keep dirty transcript search from blocking the gateway
target.body:
Closes #105735

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where searching a session with a dirty transcript index could block the Gateway event loop while the index was rebuilt.

The rebuild began synchronously inside `searchSessionTranscripts`. Its initial SQLite work, transcript parsing, and index writes ran before the async function reached its first yield. Deferring that same work with `setImmediate` would only move the stall to the next event-loop turn.

## Why This Change Was Made

Dirty-index reconciliation now runs in a packaged worker, while transcript search returns promptly with `indexing: true`.

The worker plans outside transactions and applies short, bounded write batches protected by a database-owned claim generation. Transcript mutations invalidate an active claim, and reconciliation performs a final authoritative revision check before clearing the dirty state.

A process-wide single-slot queue bounds worker concurrency. Planning and write progress have separate watchdogs; failure or timeout releases the slot for a later retry. There is no large synchronous fallback when worker startup fails.

Normal clean-index searches and synchronous indexing of ordinary transcript appends are unchanged.

## User Impact

Gateway requests and timers remain responsive while a dirty transcript index is rebuilt. Once reconciliation finishes, transcript search returns the correctly rebuilt index.

Concurrent appends, rewinds, replacements, deletions, and reconciliation attempts cannot incorrectly mark stale index contents clean.

## Evidence

Focused regression and packaging tests:

```text
OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
  src/config/sessions/session-transcript-search.test.ts \
  src/infra/tsdown-config.test.ts \
  --reporter=verbose \
  --maxWorkers=1
```

Result: 38 tests passed.

The regression coverage proves:

- Event-loop heartbeats continue after reconciliation is actively underway.
- Search eventually returns the rebuilt transcript index.
- Two database connections cannot concurrently own the same rebuild.
- Append, rewind, same-count replacement, and deletion races invalidate stale work.
- Large unrelated FTS contents do not cause long write-lock scans.
- Abandoned claims and nonresponding workers recover through bounded timeouts.
- Source, stable distribution, and hashed distribution worker paths resolve correctly.

Additional validation:

- `pnpm build` passed and emitted the transcript reconciliation worker.
- `pnpm check` passed.
- Fresh branch-mode autoreview against `origin/main` completed with no actionable findings.

## Suggested Review Order

1. `src/config/sessions/session-transcript-reconcile.ts` — claim lifecycle, planning, bounded writes, and final authoritative check.
2. `src/config/sessions/session-transcript-search.ts` — worker queue, deduplication, watchdogs, and search behavior.
3. `src/config/sessions/session-transcript-index.ts` — transcript mutations invalidating active claims.
4. `src/config/sessions/session-transcript-search.test.ts` — responsiveness, concurrency, race, and recovery proof.
5. `src/config/sessions/session-transcript-reconcile.worker.ts` — worker entry and message settlement.
6. `tsdown.config.ts`, `scripts/release-check.ts`, and `src/infra/tsdown-config.test.ts` — packaging and release inventory.

## AI Assistance

This change was developed with Codex assistance. The implementation was reviewed against repository guidance, validated with focused regression tests plus build/check gates, and passed a fresh branch-mode autoreview.

## Real behavior proof

Exact head `af68cb535507a379b18fe12c4c72c8b95b5f7f2f` was exercised through a real packaged Gateway process and its WebSocket RPC boundary using a temporary state directory. The setup used 100,000 synthetic transcript message events, then removed only the derived FTS and index-state rows to reproduce a dirty upgrade/rebuild state. No model or provider call was involved.

Redacted client transcript:

```text
{"event":"initial_search","gatewayRpcMs":687,"indexing":true,"resultCount":0}
{"event":"gateway_turn","turn":1,"healthRpcMs":194,"healthResponded":true,"searchRpcMs":351,"indexing":true,"resultCount":0}
{"event":"gateway_turn","turn":2,"healthRpcMs":5,"healthResponded":true,"searchRpcMs":311,"indexing":true,"resultCount":0}
{"event":"gateway_turn","turn":3,"healthRpcMs":3,"healthResponded":true,"searchRpcMs":275,"indexing":true,"resultCount":0}
{"event":"gateway_turn","turn":4,"healthRpcMs":4,"healthResponded":true,"searchRpcMs":251,"indexing":true,"resultCount":0}
{"event":"gateway_turn","turn":5,"healthRpcMs":3,"healthResponded":true,"searchRpcMs":272,"indexing":true,"resultCount":0}
{"event":"initial_search","gatewayRpcMs":885,"indexing":false,"resultCount":1}
{"event":"gateway_turn","turn":1,"healthRpcMs":11,"healthResponded":true,"searchRpcMs":1068,"indexing":false,"resultCount":1}
```

This demonstrates that unrelated Gateway health requests continued completing over multiple turns while reconciliation was actively reporting `indexing: true`, and that the same real RPC later converged to the rebuilt search result. The Gateway then shut down cleanly and the synthetic state was removed.

target.title: fix(telegram): bound stalled diagnostic response reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Telegram diagnostics and membership audits could keep waiting after the Bot API returned response headers but then stalled or only trickled the response body.

## Why This Change Was Made

Telegram Bot API diagnostic body reads now use a Telegram-local bounded reader with the existing byte cap, a per-chunk idle timeout, and an overall body deadline. The change covers `getMe`, best-effort `getWebhookInfo`, and membership-audit `getChatMember` reads without changing fetch/header timeout or webhook best-effort semantics.

## User Impact

Telegram setup checks and membership audits now fail or degrade on a bounded deadline instead of appearing to spin forever on a stuck response body.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/telegram/src/response-body-timeout.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/probe.response-body-timeout.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/probe.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/audit.test.ts` (22 tests passed)
- `git diff --check upstream/main..HEAD`
- Claude autoreview: clean, no accepted/actionable findings
### Exact-head controlled-network proof

Exact head: `f174acb7b443a366fed7048448884d226dab886f`.

Command:

```text

It called production `probeTelegram()` and `auditTelegramGroupMembership()` through the production Telegram undici transport, routing only the Bot API root to a loopback `node:http` server. It used a redacted fake token, no mocked adapter, no real Telegram traffic, and no credentials.

target.title: fix(gateway): add base64 validation before decode in talk-realtime-relay
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes #105846

**Problem**: Real-time relay audio frames use unpadded base64 encoding, but the `isValidBase64` guard from `chat-attachments.ts` requires length % 4 === 0, rejecting valid unpadded audio frames. This breaks relay clients sending standard unpadded base64.

**Solution**: Replace the custom `isValidRelayBase64` with `canonicalizeBase64` from `@openclaw/media-core/base64`. The canonical helper already accepts unpadded base64 (auto-pads), strips whitespace, and rejects invalid characters — exactly the behavior needed for relay audio frames from browser APIs, without introducing a second base64 policy.

**What changed**: In `src/gateway/talk-realtime-relay.ts` — removed the custom `isValidRelayBase64` function and `isBase64DataCharCode` import. Added `canonicalizeBase64` import from `@openclaw/media-core/base64`. Changed the guard on `sendTalkRealtimeRelayAudio` from `isValidRelayBase64` to `canonicalizeBase64`. No changes to `chat-attachments.ts` (the exports belong to PR #105837).

**NOT changed**: No changes to relay session lifecycle, audio processing, `sendTalkRealtimeRelayAudio` signature, or any other gateway logic. No new base64 policies introduced — the canonical media-core helper is the single source of truth.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Canonical base64 validation for real-time relay audio frames using `canonicalizeBase64` from `@openclaw/media-core/base64` — accepts unpadded base64, strips whitespace, rejects invalid input.
**Real environment tested**: Linux x64, Node.js 25.9.0, OpenClaw `main@HEAD` with this patch applied.
**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: `node --import tsx/esm -e "..."` (standalone validation against production `canonicalizeBase64`)
**After-fix evidence**: 5/5 validation scenarios passed with whitespace handling (see terminal output below).
**Observed result after the fix**: Valid padded base64 returns canonical form (defined), valid unpadded base64 auto-padded to canonical form (defined) — key behavior for relay audio, empty string rejected (undefined), invalid characters rejected (undefined), padding-in-middle rejected (undefined), whitespace stripped.
**What was not tested**: End-to-end relay session with real audio provider (requires full Gateway runtime); the canonical helper is already tested via `packages/media-core/src/base64.test.ts` (7 tests pass).

## Tests and validation

```
$ node --import tsx/esm -e "..."

=== Real behavior proof: canonicalizeBase64 for relay audio ===
(Replaces custom isValidRelayBase64 with canonical media-core helper)

  PASS canonicalizeBase64("dGVzdA==") → "dGVzdA==" (expected defined)
  PASS canonicalizeBase64("dGVzdA") → "dGVzdA==" (expected defined)
  PASS canonicalizeBase64("") → undefined (expected undefined)
  PASS canonicalizeBase64("invalid!") → undefined (expected undefined)
  PASS canonicalizeBase64("abc=defg") → undefined (expected undefined)

Whitespace tolerance (relay frames may have trailing newlines):
  canonicalizeBase64("dGVzdA== ") → "dGVzdA=="
  canonicalizeBase64("SGV s bG8= ") → "SGVsbG8="

5/5 passed, whitespace OK
```

Comparison with previous `isValidRelayBase64`:

| Behavior | `isValidRelayBase64` (removed) | `canonicalizeBase64` (new) |
|----------|-------------------------------|---------------------------|
| Padded `"dGVzdA=="` | ✅ accept | ✅ accept |
| Unpadded `"dGVzdA"` | ✅ accept | ✅ accept (auto-pads) |
| Empty `""` | ❌ reject | ❌ reject (undefined) |
| Invalid chars `"invalid!"` | ❌ reject | ❌ reject (undefined) |
| Padding mid `"abc=defg"` | ❌ reject | ❌ reject (undefined) |
| Whitespace tolerance | ❌ not handled | ✅ stripped |

Existing media-core tests pass, and new focused relay guard tests exercise the actual `sendTalkRealtimeRelayAudio` entry point:

```
$ pnpm test src/gateway/talk-realtime-relay.guard.test.ts --reporter=verbose

 ✓ relay audio base64 guard > accepts valid unpadded base64 audio frame
 ✓ relay audio base64 guard > accepts valid padded base64 audio frame
 ✓ relay audio base64 guard > rejects empty audio frame
 ✓ relay audio base64 guard > rejects malformed base64 audio frame

 Test Files  4 passed (4)
      Tests  16 passed (16)
```

All 16 tests pass across 4 gateway shards, proving the `canonicalizeBase64` guard works correctly at the relay entry point.

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible — valid padded base64 continues to work; unpadded base64 is now also accepted as intended
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [ ] I have updated relevant documentation
- [x] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary

---
merge-risk: 🦺 low — uses existing canonical media-core helper (`canonicalizeBase64`) instead of introducing a new base64 policy; previously-rejected valid unpadded inputs are now accepted, which is the intended fix.

## Summary

Fixes #105837

**Problem**: `persistInboundImagesForTranscript` decodes base64 image data via `Buffer.from(data, "base64")` without validating the encoding first. Malformed base64 can silently produce garbage bytes or unexpected errors.

**Solution**: Add `isValidBase64` guard before decode, throwing a clear error message when the image data is not valid base64. Export `isValidBase64` from the module so it can be tested directly against the production implementation.

**What changed**: One guard in `src/gateway/chat-attachments.ts:74` — `if (!isValidBase64(image.data))` before `Buffer.from` decode. Exported both `isValidBase64` and `isBase64DataCharCode` (previously module-private) to enable direct production testing. Rewrote `chat-attachments.base64.test.ts` to import and validate against the exported production function instead of using placeholder assertions and a reimplemented copy.

**NOT changed**: No changes to existing test behavior, no changes to image persistence logic, no changes to error handling outside this new guard. All existing tests continue to pass. The existing placeholder tests were replaced entirely with real assertions against the production function.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: `isValidBase64` guard validates base64 before `Buffer.from` decode in `persistInboundImagesForTranscript`.
**Real environment tested**: Linux x64, Node.js 25.9.0, OpenClaw `main@HEAD` with this patch applied.
**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: `node --import tsx/esm -e "..."` (simulates the guard+decode path of `persistInboundImagesForTranscript`)
**After-fix evidence**: 6/6 scenarios passed (see terminal output below).
**Observed result after the fix**: Valid 1x1 PNG image passes guard and decodes to 70 bytes; malformed/empty/unpadded inputs are all rejected by the guard before reaching `Buffer.from`.
**What was not tested**: End-to-end Gateway server with actual multipart uploads (requires full runtime); the guard+decode path is exactly what `persistInboundImagesForTranscript` does at lines 73-75.

## Tests and validation

target.title: fix(agents): tighten grepSchema context/limit from Type.Number to Type.Integer
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes #105822

**Problem**: `grepSchema.context` and `grepSchema.limit` use `Type.Number`, accepting fractional values like `1.5` or `10.5` that are semantically invalid for context lines and match counts.

**Solution**: Change both fields to `Type.Integer` so schema validation rejects floats before reaching tool logic, and export `grepSchema` so the unit test validates against the production schema rather than a reconstructed copy. Importing `grepSchema` from the grep module is safe for a unit test because the schema is a plain TypeBox object with no runtime side effects. target.title: fix(ui): catalog sessions select in place and continue from desktop-app sources
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

External Codex/Claude Code sessions surfaced in the Control UI sidebar ("session catalog") were effectively unusable:

1. **Wrongly view-only.** Almost every real Claude Code session on the gateway host showed "This external session source is view-only." Two causes:
   - Sessions driven through the Claude Code **desktop app** are recorded with `source: "claude-desktop"` during catalog discovery, and the anthropic plugin hard-required `source === "claude-cli"` for `canContinue`/continue — even though desktop sessions live in the same `~/.claude/projects` JSONL store (discovery drops desktop records without one) and `claude --resume --fork-session` continues them identically.
   - The chat pane showed the view-only banner whenever catalog metadata wasn't loaded yet (or the lookup failed), so even continuable sessions flashed or stuck as "view-only".
2. **Selection lifted the session into the chats block.** Clicking a catalog row synthesized a phantom row in the regular sessions list labeled with the raw `catalog:claude:gateway%3Alocal:…` key (deep-link fallback in `resolveSessionNavigation`), and previously adopted sessions rendered twice — once in the catalog group and once in the regular list, jumping to the top on activity. Catalog rows also never showed a selected state.
3. **"Local Codex" / "Local Claude" noise.** Rows carried the gateway-host label as subtitle whenever a catalog had more than one host, adding no signal (the group header already names the source).

## Why This Change Was Made

Catalog sessions should feel like regular sessions that happen to run through Codex/Claude Code: click → selected in place, transcript shown, type → continue with streaming. All gating now keys off the provider-reported per-session `canContinue`, so paired-node continuation (PR #105833) lights up in this UI automatically once it lands.

## User Impact

- Local Claude Code sessions (CLI **and** desktop app) are continuable from the web UI: type into the transcript view, the session is adopted, and the reply streams in.
- The view-only banner only appears when the provider actually reports the session as non-continuable; nothing flashes during load.
- Clicking a catalog session selects it in place. No phantom `catalog:…` row, no duplicate entry jumping to the top of the chats list. Adopted sessions render as full session rows (run spinner, unread dot, pin/menu actions) inside their catalog group, bound immediately on adoption via a `openclaw-session-catalog-continued` event instead of waiting for the next 30s poll.
- Host subtitles only show a paired node's machine name; "Local Codex"/"Local Claude" subtitles are gone.

## Evidence

- Live verification against a scratch gateway built from this branch on a Mac with 40 real Claude Code sessions (mixed CLI/desktop): before, every session showed the view-only banner + phantom raw-key row on click; after, rows select in place, the composer is enabled, and `sessions.catalog.list` reports `canContinue: true` for desktop-source sessions.
- New tests:
  - `extensions/anthropic/session-catalog.test.ts` — desktop-source rows list as continuable and adopt with the same one-shot fork binding.
  - `ui/src/lib/sessions/navigation.test.ts` — no synthesized row for catalog session keys.
  - `ui/src/components/app-sidebar.test.ts` — node-only host subtitles; in-place active highlight without a phantom chat row; adopted rows render once (as live rows) inside the catalog group; catalog-continued event binds the adopted key immediately.
- `ui/src/lib/sessions/navigation.test.ts` (12/12) and `extensions/anthropic/session-catalog.test.ts` pass locally; full suite via hosted CI on this PR.

target.body:
Closes #105959

AI-assisted. I reviewed the affected runtime paths and understand the changes. A redacted agent transcript is omitted unless maintainers request one.

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a maintenance problem where core production code exposed 111 distinct `OPENCLAW_*` environment-variable reads, including undocumented aliases and test controls that duplicated canonical config, upstream variables, or injected seams.

## Why This Change Was Made

This audits the entire baseline surface and removes only seven undocumented variables with no docs, installer, extension, workflow, or named packaged-runtime contract. Documented variables remain unchanged. Ambiguous user-facing variables remain as explicit follow-up decisions instead of being silently removed.

Removed paths:

- three OpenClaw-prefixed ClawHub aliases; canonical `CLAWHUB_*` variables remain
- terminal clear/cursor overrides; persisted settings remain canonical

target.title: fix(qa-lab): close transport before gateway teardown
target.body:
Closes #106005

## What Problem This Solves

QA Smoke scenarios can finish successfully while Crabline transport work is still delivering an HTTP response. The suite stopped the gateway first, so that in-flight delivery became an unhandled `HTTP response closed before delivery completed` rejection.

## Why This Change Was Made

Close the transport before stopping the gateway. Transport cleanup drains outstanding provider HTTP work while the gateway can still accept delivery. The cleanup-order regression test preserves that ordering even when cleanup reports an error.

## User Impact

QA Smoke no longer reports a post-success unhandled rejection caused by its own teardown order. Runtime behavior outside QA Lab is unchanged.

## Evidence

- Exact-head focused QA extension suite on `fd41dc3f1c600cd948e37f97a2078122ebde868b`: 29 passed.
- Exact-head QA smoke on the QA Lab gateway plus `qa-channel` transport: `channel-chat-baseline` passed 1/1; the captured output reached `CRABBOX_PHASE:complete` and explicitly confirmed `TEARDOWN_REJECTION:absent`.

- Formatting and type-aware OXLint passed for the two changed files.
- Fresh autoreview found no in-scope actionable findings.

target.title: fix(discord): bound stalled probe response reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Discord probe checks could hang after the `getMe` request returned response headers but the JSON response body stopped producing data.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Discord probe now reads the successful `getMe` JSON body through the bounded response reader with the existing 16 MiB cap and a per-chunk timeout tied to the probe timeout. Existing non-OK handling, malformed JSON wording, and probe result flow are preserved.

## User Impact

Discord configuration checks now fail quickly on a stalled probe body instead of leaving users waiting on an unbounded read.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/discord/src/probe.intents.test.ts` (10 tests passed)
- `git diff --check upstream/main..HEAD`
- Claude autoreview: clean, no accepted/actionable findings
### Exact-head controlled-network proof

Exact head: `f6de53aba381701e59a0554a8ffe80c9c5b76457`.

Command:

```text
PROOF_HEAD=f6de53aba381701e59a0554a8ffe80c9c5b76457 HTTP_PROXY= HTTPS_PROXY= http_proxy= https_proxy= ALL_PROXY= all_proxy= NO_PROXY=127.0.0.1,localhost no_proxy=127.0.0.1,localhost timeout 30s node --import tsx scratchpad/discord-probe-current-head-proof.mts
```

The temporary harness was removed after the run. It called production `probeDiscord()`, using the existing fetch seam only to route Discord API URLs to a loopback `node:http` server. The underlying client was real Node fetch; no mocked `Response`, Discord traffic, or credentials were used.

Redacted transcript:

```text
proof: exact-head=f6de53aba381701e59a0554a8ffe80c9c5b76457 production Discord probe
probe: mode=normal ok=true error=null bot=bot-1 elapsed=42ms
[fetch-timeout] fetch timeout after 120ms operation=fetchWithTimeout
probe: mode=header-stall ok=false error=request timed out elapsed=196ms
server: response closed mode=header-stall writableEnded=false
probe: mode=body-stall ok=false error=discord.probe.getMe: JSON response stalled after 120ms elapsed=129ms
server: response closed mode=body-stall writableEnded=false
probe: mode=slow-trickle ok=true error=null bot=bot-1 elapsed=1450ms
probe: mode=normal ok=true error=null bot=bot-1 elapsed=3ms
proof: current-head real HTTP assertions passed
```

Observed: a request stalled before headers aborts and closes its socket; a response that sends headers and a partial JSON body and then stops aborts through the production probe reader and closes its socket; a later normal probe succeeds. All assertions passed; exit 0.

Known limits: this is controlled local HTTP transport proof, not live Discord. Current head enforces an idle/per-chunk timeout, not a total response deadline: a body sending one chunk every 40 ms completed after 1450 ms with `timeoutMs=120`. This proof therefore establishes cleanup for a body that stops producing data and does not claim protection from an indefinitely slow trickle. The exact command referenced a temporary uncommitted harness that has been removed.

target.title: fix(telegram): catch unhandled rejections in webhook and ingress worker shutdown
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes two channel reliability bugs in the Telegram plugin where shutdown paths can produce unhandled promise rejections, which Node.js terminates the process for by default:

1. **Webhook shutdown**: if `bot.stop()` rejected during abort-triggered shutdown, the rejection was unhandled (`void shutdown()`), crashing the process.
2. **Ingress worker stop**: `stop()` was not idempotent, so calling it twice could post a second `stop` message and leak a second 15s terminate timer. If `worker.terminate()` rejected, the rejection was unhandled.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Webhook**: catch shutdown errors in both the pre-aborted path and the abort listener, route them to `runtime.error`, and continue owned cleanup (transport close, status, diagnostics) in a `finally` block even if `bot.stop()` rejects.
- **Ingress worker**: guard `stop()` with a `stopped` flag for idempotency, catch `postMessage` errors for already-terminated workers, and catch `worker.terminate()` rejections.

## User Impact

No more unhandled rejection crashes during Telegram channel restart or shutdown.

## Evidence

### Tests

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/telegram/src/webhook.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/telegram-ingress-worker.test.ts -- --run
```

```
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  38 passed (38)
```

### Negative Control Proof

**Webhook shutdown rejection handling**:

```bash
# Step 1: Revert to origin/main version
git checkout origin/main -- extensions/telegram/src/webhook.ts

# Step 2: Run test - Expected: FAIL with Unhandled Rejection
pnpm test extensions/telegram/src/webhook.test.ts -- --run -t "does not leak unhandled rejections when shutdown throws"
```

Result: ❌ **FAILED** - Unhandled Rejection: Error: bot stop failed

```bash
# Step 3: Restore fix
git checkout HEAD -- extensions/telegram/src/webhook.ts

# Step 4: Run test - Expected: PASS
pnpm test extensions/telegram/src/webhook.test.ts -- --run -t "does not leak unhandled rejections when shutdown throws"
```

Result: ✅ **PASSED** - 1 passed

**Ingress worker stop idempotency**:

```bash
# Step 1: Revert to origin/main version
git checkout origin/main -- extensions/telegram/src/telegram-ingress-worker.ts

# Step 2: Run test - Expected: FAIL
pnpm test extensions/telegram/src/telegram-ingress-worker.test.ts -- --run
```

Result: ❌ **FAILED** - AssertionError: expected Promise{…} to be Promise{…} (stop() not idempotent)

```bash
# Step 3: Restore fix
git checkout HEAD -- extensions/telegram/src/telegram-ingress-worker.ts

# Step 4: Run test - Expected: ALL PASS
pnpm test extensions/telegram/src/telegram-ingress-worker.test.ts -- --run
```

Result: ✅ **PASSED** - 2 passed

### Changes

- `extensions/telegram/src/webhook.ts`: catch shutdown errors in abort paths, log via `runtime.error`, continue cleanup in `finally`
- `extensions/telegram/src/webhook.test.ts`: new test for shutdown rejection handling
- `extensions/telegram/src/telegram-ingress-worker.ts`: idempotent `stop()` with shared stop promise, catch `postMessage` and `terminate` errors
- `extensions/telegram/src/telegram-ingress-worker.test.ts`: new tests for stop idempotency and terminate rejection handling

---

target.title: feat(mobile): default pairing to full node access
target.body:
Closes #105843

## What Problem This Solves

The official iOS and Android apps connected as nodes, but mobile QR/setup-code pairing only handed them a bounded operator credential. Users therefore missed normal full node/operator behavior unless they manually approved more access, and native settings did not explain the limited state or upgrade path.

## Why This Change Was Made

Official mobile pairing now issues the node credential plus full operator access by default. Full access is restricted to the exact official mobile bootstrap profile and matching native client metadata; arbitrary bootstrap profiles remain bounded. Control UI and `openclaw qr --limited` preserve an explicit limited-access fallback, and rescanning a Full access code upgrades an existing limited mobile pairing.

## User Impact

iOS and Android pair as fully usable nodes by default. Operators who prefer least privilege can choose Limited access, while both native settings screens show Full/Limited state and tell limited users to rescan a Full access QR code to upgrade.

## Evidence

- Blacksmith Testbox `tbx_01kxckgwbgms3d3n72gc5kpkky` (`violet-barnacle-a620`): `pnpm check:changed` passed all selected core, core-test, UI, extension, app, and docs lanes in 14m07s.
- Gateway authorization suites: 82/82 passed; includes full handoff, bounded limited credential verification, and same-identity limited-to-full upgrade.
- CLI setup: 24/24 passed; black-box default/`--limited` exercise reported Full/Limited respectively, issued non-empty distinct setup codes, and exposed no credential values.
- Control UI Chromium E2E passed; recorded request sequence `full -> limited -> full -> full`, proving regeneration and reset-on-reopen. Before/after artifacts retained in the Testbox run.
- Android: `pnpm android:lint` and `pnpm android:test` passed (34 Gradle tasks). Native i18n generation/check, protocol/Swift generation checks, and targeted SwiftFormat passed.
- Fresh Autoreview slices: core, authorization-sensitive gateway handler, native apps, Control UI, and regression tests all clean after accepted findings were fixed.
- Source-blind behavior validation found no product failures across executable CLI/UI/upgrade paths. Direct iOS runtime proof was blocked because the approved Apple host was unreachable over SSH; macOS CI remains the Apple gate.

target.title: fix(commitments): avoid quadratic heartbeat session discovery
target.body:
Related: #105787

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes heartbeat commitment fan-out latency when many due commitments belong to one session. The existing path loads and expires the JSON store while holding the queue/file lock, releases that lock, then scans the returned in-memory records. For every qualifying due record it rescans the complete store to count recent sent commitments. The quadratic scan is outside the lock, but it delays heartbeat processing and increases heartbeat latency. Reported isolated medians were approximately 191 ms at 1,000, 847 ms at 2,000, and 2.28 s at 4,000 records.

## Why This Change Was Made

The commitments store now builds the rolling 24-hour sent-count map once per agent and reuses it for due-session discovery and single-session due selection. Due-window, snooze, expiry, daily-cap, ordering, limit, agent-scope, queue, and cross-process file-lock behavior remain on the existing path.

This is intentionally an interim JSON-store fix. OpenClaw's shared SQLite state schema already contains a commitments table and indexes, but making it canonical requires a separate JSON-to-SQLite migration/doctor contract and broader persistence coverage. That migration remains a follow-up rather than expanding this focused latency fix.

## User Impact

Heartbeat commitment discovery changes from repeated full-store counting to one aggregation pass plus the existing due-record scan. Large concentrated sessions therefore scale linearly with store size instead of quadratically, without changing which sessions are eligible for delivery.

## Evidence

- Store correctness coverage includes due windows, snoozes, rolling daily caps, agent scope, deterministic session-key ordering, expiry, and concurrent file-store updates.
- The concentrated-session regression uses 8,000 due records in one session and a production-like `limit: 10`, so the base implementation repeatedly rescans the store while the fixed implementation reuses one count map.
- The runner-level regression uses the production heartbeat runner with a real temporary JSON state directory and 16,000 concentrated due records. The model and channel boundaries are stubbed there for deterministic CI coverage.
- Focused validation, using the linked-worktree local fallback:
  ```text
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/commitments/store.test.ts src/infra/heartbeat-runner.commitments.test.ts --reporter=verbose
  11 store tests passed; 14 heartbeat-runner tests passed.
  ```

### Real Gateway heartbeat proof

I reran the actual built `dist/index.js gateway` locally in fresh isolated state directories for the baseline and PR. Each run seeded 16,000 pending due commitments plus one recent sent commitment, all concentrated in one Telegram session, then invoked the production Gateway `wake` RPC once. The Gateway scheduler, heartbeat runner, JSON store, due-session selector, Telegram plugin dispatch, and delivery/status updates were real. The model and Telegram Bot API were local HTTP fixtures, so the run was secretless and deterministic; no scheduler, store, runner, or channel-dispatch function was stubbed.

The baseline used main checkout `43901be298`, a descendant of the PR base `6c884691105b`; there were no changes under `src/commitments/` or `src/infra/heartbeat-runner.ts` between those refs. The PR run used `fcb249f4953485071e123b7cd2fce31f32ea96da`. The redacted terminal output below is one matched run per revision:

```text
baseline 43901be298:
REAL_GATEWAY_HEARTBEAT_PROOF {"store":"json","commitmentCount":16000,"seededDueSessionKeys":["agent:main:telegram:proof"],"channelSendCount":1,"sentRequestBodies":1,"elapsedMs":21510,"pendingAfterRun":15998,"lastHeartbeat":{"status":"sent","to":"telegram:12345","durationMs":1947}}

PR fcb249f495:
REAL_GATEWAY_HEARTBEAT_PROOF {"store":"json","commitmentCount":16000,"seededDueSessionKeys":["agent:main:telegram:proof"],"channelSendCount":1,"sentRequestBodies":1,"elapsedMs":13990,"pendingAfterRun":15998,"lastHeartbeat":{"status":"sent","to":"telegram:12345","durationMs":2267}}
```

Selection and delivery behavior matched: both runs discovered the same session key, sent exactly one Telegram request to the same target, reported `sent`, and left the same 15,998 commitments pending. Wake-to-delivery elapsed time was 21.5 s on the baseline and 14.0 s on the PR. This is representative real-process behavior proof, not a statistically stable benchmark; cold Gateway startup and local fixture variance affect timing. The durable scaling proof remains the concentrated-session regression.

### Direct DigitalOcean proof status

I attempted the requested direct DigitalOcean route with the token supplied through the environment and never printed it:

```text

target.title: fix(gateway): always enforce path containment for session transcript archive
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `archiveSessionTranscriptsDetailed` used a single `dirname(storePath)` containment root after removing the opt-in `restrictToStoreDir` flag. This dropped valid custom transcript paths (when `storePath` is undefined) and cross-agent candidate paths, breaking the existing resolver contract.

**Solution**: Replace the single-root filter with multi-root containment matching the resolver's validated candidate boundary. The archive function now accepts candidates from the store directory, sibling agent sessions directories, and the legacy global sessions directory.

**What changed**: `archiveSessionTranscriptsDetailed` now uses a `containmentRoots` array built from the same inputs as `resolveSessionTranscriptCandidates`. Each candidate is accepted if it falls under any root. 4 new regression tests cover cross-agent, no-store custom, and poisoned path scenarios. Total: 396 tests passed.

**What did NOT change**: Function signatures remain the same (callers unchanged). Existing archive behavior for normal store-path sessions is preserved. The `restrictToStoreDir` parameter is kept as a no-op for backward compatibility. No changes to the resolver (`resolveSessionTranscriptCandidates`) or path validation logic (`resolvePathWithinSessionsDir`).

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Session transcript archive containment now matches the resolver boundary, preserving custom and cross-agent paths while rejecting poisoned paths.

**Real environment tested**: Linux 4.19.112, Node 22.19.0, pnpm 11.2.2

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
npx tsx /tmp/archive-proof.mjs
```
L2 real behavior proof: direct function call with real filesystem state.

**After-fix evidence**:
```
=== Before ===

cross-agent transcript exists: true

target.title: fix(gmail): stop watcher when OAuth renewal is invalid
target.body:
Closes #96088

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running the Gmail watcher could keep a `gog gmail watch serve` process alive after Gmail watch renewal failed with terminal OAuth errors such as `invalid_grant` or revoked credentials. That made the watcher look live even though Gmail watch coverage could no longer be renewed.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Gmail watcher now classifies `gog watch start` failures as retryable or terminal. Retryable watch-start failures keep the existing serve-and-renew behavior, while terminal OAuth failures refuse initial startup or stop the active watcher with a clear re-authentication reason. The same classification is shared by the Gateway auto-start watcher and the foreground `openclaw webhooks gmail run` path.

## User Impact

Operators now get a stopped or non-started Gmail watcher when credentials need re-authentication instead of a stale listener that appears healthy. Transient Gmail watch-start failures still keep the previous retry path.

## Evidence

target.title: feat(control-ui): agent identity editor, Settings-homed Agents page, scalable chip switcher
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a set of Control UI problems around agent identity and navigation:

- Agents with no configured identity show their raw id (for example `main`) in the sidebar chip and chat, and there is no way to set an agent's display name, emoji, or avatar image from the web UI at all. The identity plumbing (`agents.update`, identity config, workspace `IDENTITY.md`, avatar serving) already exists server-side but is not exposed.
- The Agents management page lives in the customizable sidebar nav ("More" menu) even though it is configuration, while Settings already has an "AI & Agents" group. Settings placement was inconsistent.
- The sidebar agent-chip switcher renders every agent as a flat list, which does not scale past a handful of agents, and there is no way to reach agent management from the chip.
- Sidebar chrome (nav labels, session rows, the chip) is text-selectable, so drag interactions select label text and read as broken.

## Why This Change Was Made

The identity editor writes through the existing `agents.update` RPC, which persists to `agents.list[].identity` and rewrites the workspace `IDENTITY.md` — so the agent itself and the UI share one identity source, and an agent can still change its own name/emoji/avatar by editing that file. Avatar uploads are downscaled client-side (256px WebP/PNG data URL) so the persisted config stays small and within the existing 2 MB avatar policy.

The Agents page moves under Settings (`/settings/agents`, old `/agents` kept as an alias) into the existing Agents group, following the same `definePage` alias pattern as other settings slices. The chip menu becomes the primary switcher: above ten agents it shows pinned agents first plus an inline filter over the full roster; pins persist like the existing sidebar nav pins (browser-profile scoped). A new "Agent settings" row deep-links to the selected agent via `?agent=`.

## User Impact

- Agents page Overview tab gains an Identity card: display name, emoji, and avatar image upload with live preview; saving updates the sidebar chip, chat, and `IDENTITY.md`.
- Agents now lives in Settings → Agents; `/agents` URLs still work. Sidebar "More" menu no longer lists it.
- Agent chip menu: "Agent settings" row; rosters >10 agents get pinned-first rows and a find-agent filter. Pin/unpin from the Agents page toolbar.
- Sidebar text is no longer selectable (inputs inside menus still are).

## Evidence

- New/updated jsdom tests: `ui/src/components/app-sidebar.test.ts` (agent-settings navigation row, ≤10 plain roster, pinned+filter behavior, no-pin fallback), `ui/src/app/settings.node.test.ts` (pinned-agent persistence + normalization), `ui/src/app-navigation.test.ts` (route table + settings groups).
- Live verification on a production gateway (source checkout): setting `identity.name`/`identity.emoji` via the same config path immediately renders the sidebar chip as the configured name with emoji avatar (gateway hot-reloads config; no restart).
- Docs updated: `docs/web/control-ui.md` (footer chip/switcher paragraph, Settings → Agents bullet with identity editing and `IDENTITY.md` note).

target.title: fix: active-memory recalls from all agents serialize on one shared lane
target.body:
Related: #72015 (this addresses the recall-lane serialization portion of that report; the QMD boot-initialization portion is separate)

> This PR is AI-assisted: the analysis, patch, and test update were written with an AI coding agent. A human operator reviewed the change and validated it against a live deployment.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where, on multi-agent gateways, memory recall runs from different agents queue behind each other. The active-memory recall subagent always enqueues on the single shared `active-memory` lane, and command lanes default to `maxConcurrent: 1`, so every agent's recall serializes globally. The lane wait burns the recall's turn-scoped time budget, so under concurrent traffic (several agents active at once, or a burst of session resets) recalls run late, time out, or are skipped, and users see replies without memory context.

## Why This Change Was Made

Key the recall lane by agent id (`active-memory:<agentId>`) so recalls serialize per agent instead of across the whole gateway. Lanes are created lazily on first use, so no lane registration change is needed. `agentId` is already a required parameter at the enqueue site. Single-agent deployments behave exactly as before (one agent, one lane).

## User Impact

On multi-agent gateways, one agent's memory recall no longer delays every other agent's. Recall latency under concurrent load drops and fewer recall time budgets are exhausted while queued, so memory injection lands more reliably. No configuration change; single-agent installs see no behavioral difference.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-active-memory.config.ts extensions/active-memory/index.test.ts` passes 154/154, including the updated lane assertion (agent `main` now enqueues on `active-memory:main`).
- Live observation motivating the fix: on a multi-agent gateway, recall queue-wait clusters coincided with degraded or skipped memory injection whenever several agents were active in the same window; single-agent sessions on the same build were unaffected.
- Full `pnpm build` / `pnpm check` deferred to CI (memory-constrained local host).



## Runtime evidence (real behavior, redacted)

The submitting gateway has been running this change backported onto v2026.6.10 since 2026-07-05, on a small multi-agent fleet. The excerpt below (agent names and the room id redacted, timestamps UTC, lines otherwise verbatim) shows two agents' Active Memory recall sub-runs executing concurrently in the same group room:

```
07:49:22.780Z active-memory: agent=agent-a session=agent:agent-a:slack:group:<room> start timeoutMs=15000
07:49:24.458Z active-memory: agent=agent-b session=agent:agent-b:slack:group:<room> start timeoutMs=15000
07:49:28.310Z active-memory: agent=agent-a session=agent:agent-a:slack:group:<room> done status=ok elapsedMs=5530
07:49:42.790Z active-memory: agent=agent-b session=agent:agent-b:slack:group:<room> done status=ok elapsedMs=18332
```

Why this demonstrates per-agent lanes rather than enqueue timing: `elapsedMs` equals the wall-clock delta between each start/done pair (agent-a 22.780 to 28.310 is 5530 ms; agent-b 24.458 to 42.790 is 18332 ms), so the `start` line marks actual execution start, not queue admission. agent-b began executing 3.9 s into agent-a's 5.5 s run. Under the pre-patch shared lane (`maxConcurrent: 1`) the second recall cannot start before the first finishes; overlapping execution is only possible with distinct lanes. Lane names are not printed at info level, so the proof is behavioral rather than a lane-key string.

Stability over the most recent two days of logs on the final-head behavior: 23 recall sub-runs across 3 active agents, 10 `status=ok`, 13 `status=no_relevant_memory`, zero timeouts, zero errors, elapsed 1.3 to 19.6 s (average 8.1 s), no queue backlog or gateway instability observed.

On the concurrency boundary question raised in review: that decision belongs to the maintainers. As one data point, this fleet has run one slot per agent for a week with several concurrently active agents and no saturation; an aggregate cap on top of agent-keyed lanes would also compose fine with this patch if preferred.

## Summary

Fixes #105846

**Problem**: Real-time relay audio frames use unpadded base64 encoding, but the `isValidBase64` guard from `chat-attachments.ts` requires length % 4 === 0, rejecting valid unpadded audio frames. This breaks relay clients sending standard unpadded base64.

**Solution**: Replace the custom `isValidRelayBase64` with `canonicalizeBase64` from `@openclaw/media-core/base64`. The canonical helper already accepts unpadded base64 (auto-pads), strips whitespace, and rejects invalid characters — exactly the behavior needed for relay audio frames from browser APIs, without introducing a second base64 policy.

**What changed**: In `src/gateway/talk-realtime-relay.ts` — removed the custom `isValidRelayBase64` function and `isBase64DataCharCode` import. Added `canonicalizeBase64` import from `@openclaw/media-core/base64`. Changed the guard on `sendTalkRealtimeRelayAudio` from `isValidRelayBase64` to `canonicalizeBase64`. No changes to `chat-attachments.ts` (the exports belong to PR #105837).

**NOT changed**: No changes to relay session lifecycle, audio processing, `sendTalkRealtimeRelayAudio` signature, or any other gateway logic. No new base64 policies introduced — the canonical media-core helper is the single source of truth.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Canonical base64 validation for real-time relay audio frames using `canonicalizeBase64` from `@openclaw/media-core/base64` — accepts unpadded base64, strips whitespace, rejects invalid input.
**Real environment tested**: Linux x64, Node.js 25.9.0, OpenClaw `main@HEAD` with this patch applied.
**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: `node --import tsx/esm -e "..."` (standalone validation against production `canonicalizeBase64`)
**After-fix evidence**: 5/5 validation scenarios passed with whitespace handling (see terminal output below).
**Observed result after the fix**: Valid padded base64 returns canonical form (defined), valid unpadded base64 auto-padded to canonical form (defined) — key behavior for relay audio, empty string rejected (undefined), invalid characters rejected (undefined), padding-in-middle rejected (undefined), whitespace stripped.
**What was not tested**: End-to-end relay session with real audio provider (requires full Gateway runtime); the canonical helper is already tested via `packages/media-core/src/base64.test.ts` (7 tests pass).

```
$ node --import tsx/esm -e "..."

(Replaces custom isValidRelayBase64 with canonical media-core helper)

target.title: fix: keep yielded parent runs deferred until subagents settle
target.body:
## Summary

This change promotes yielded-parent semantics into a shared parent lifecycle classifier and routes the affected cron, subagent-registry, and Discord/source-message paths through that state instead of letting each consumer infer completion from terminal-shaped model-attempt events, missing final text, or abort-shaped control flow.

The shipped behavior is:

- yielded parent + active descendants is treated as waiting/deferred, not ordinary completion;
- yielded parent + no descendant is treated as diagnostic error;
- cron delivery waits for a real final outcome instead of counting the yielded attempt as `ok / not-delivered`;
- Discord/source-message progress remains parent-owned while the yielded parent is waiting;
- descendant settlement wakes/reconciles yielded parents through the existing continuation paths.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where parent-agent runs that spawned child sessions/subagents and then called `sessions_yield` could look finished before the parent task actually completed.

The most visible failures were:

- isolated cron `agentTurn` jobs with valid delivery targets could finish as `ok / not-delivered` because the yielded parent had no final payload yet;
- Discord source-message lifecycle could clear parent progress/done indicators while child work was still active or while the parent was waiting to reconcile final output;
- run history/status surfaces made yielded parent work look like delivery failure, ordinary success with no output, or completed source-message work instead of a paused/resumable parent lifecycle.

`session_yield` is supposed to end the current model turn, not the parent task. This PR makes that distinction explicit for the affected runtime consumers.

## User Impact / Intended Outcome

Operators and developers can now rely on `sessions_yield` after spawning child/subagent work without the parent run being misrepresented as complete at the cron or Discord lifecycle boundary.

Practically:

- autonomous development crons stop inflating misleading `ok / not-delivered` results for intentionally yielded runs;
- cron history exposes a distinct `deferred` state for yielded parent handoff;
- Discord progress no longer marks the parent source message done just because the parent yielded while children continue;
- yielded parent runs are resumed/reconciled when descendant work settles;
- debugging points to the parent/child lifecycle state instead of falsely implying delivery target resolution failed.

## Linked Context

- #95535 — `sessions_yield` isolated cron resumption/delivery gap.
- #92369 — subagent orchestration in isolated cron sessions needs reliable spawn/wait/aggregate semantics.
- #92116 — `sessions_yield` completion delivered as passive context can break orchestration loops.
- #86537 — subagent terminal reconciliation can expire suspended final delivery.
- #86538 — session write-lock timeouts can block subagent delivery lanes.
- #95833 — subagent abort-settle/session-lock failure can break session continuation.
- #92460 — isolated cron completion delivery gap around final controller return.
- #95604 — Discord subagent progress visibility.
- #94153 — durable queued subagent completion announcements.
- #95847 — requester-consumed descendant completion accounting.

## What Changes

### Shared parent lifecycle state

- Adds `src/agents/agent-lifecycle-parent-state.ts`.
- Classifies lifecycle events with explicit yielded/waiting vs terminal semantics.
- Exports the classifier through `openclaw/plugin-sdk/reply-runtime`.
- Routes subagent registry and Discord source-message handling through the classifier instead of local `yielded && paused` inference.

### Cron lifecycle and delivery

- Adds first-class cron run status `deferred`.
- Classifies yielded descendant handoff before delivery-mode branching, so text, structured payloads, `delivery.mode: none`, source-satisfied delivery, and normal direct delivery all share the same semantics.
- Prevents duplicate/interim parent announcements while descendants are active.
- Records yielded-without-descendant as explicit error diagnostic.
- Keeps deferred manual task runs active rather than failing them.
- Disables one-shot deferred cron jobs after handoff to avoid retry loops.

### Persistence, protocol, CLI, and UI

- Extends run-log JSON/SQLite encoding and status filtering for `deferred`.
- Extends Gateway protocol schemas and cron server filters.
- Extends CLI status/wait typing and docs.
- Extends hook-visible status typing.
- Adds Control UI status/filter labels and generated locale fallbacks.

### Parent/subagent reconciliation

- Tracks yielded/paused parents that still have pending descendants.
- Marks yielded parents with `wakeOnDescendantSettle` so they are resumed/reconciled when descendant work settles.
- Handles child success/failure settlement through existing subagent lifecycle recovery paths.
- Adds regression coverage for yielded parents being reconciled after child failure so diagnostics can wake the parent.

### Discord/source-message lifecycle

- Projects lifecycle events from agent execution into reply/channel handling.
- Uses the shared classifier to identify yielded/waiting parent state.
- Preserves in-progress/progress representation for yielded parents with active children.
- Avoids prematurely marking Discord status reactions done or clearing draft/progress state when the parent yielded and remains waiting.

### Concurrent user-message semantics

`docs/tools/subagents.md` documents the selected policy: if a human sends another message while a requester is yielded, the new message starts a normal turn for the same requester session. OpenClaw keeps the yielded run visible as waiting on descendant completion rather than converting it into a stale final reply; when descendant completion arrives, the completion event is handed back to the requester for synthesis.

## Implementation Notes

Implementation details are included in the What Changes section above; focused evidence and live behavior proof are preserved below.

## Tests / Verification

Focused test coverage plus type, docs, and formatting gates are preserved under Evidence below.

## Evidence

### Rebase/Squash/Proof

- Common upstream base: `13ecca5408cbc94e66105608bfe770d0fc660d76` (`origin/main`, `fix(telegram): back off session init spool retries`)
- Previous PR head: `c163d18fa610687e7dfb8585f1fe8f30b0c4185d`
- Current PR head: `73cff6aa1b0a3ab5786fdfc3a96c98f575e7fcc8`

target.title: fix(config): warn on JSON5 comment loss after successful config write
target.body:
#### What Problem This Solves

Close #105683

Fixes silent JSON5 comment loss when `openclaw.json` and its `$include`-referenced files are written back to disk. OpenClaw parses user configurations with JSON5 (supporting `//` and `/* */` comments), but the canonical write path serializes with `JSON.stringify`, which irreversibly strips all user-authored comments, documentation, and commented-out settings on every automatic config mutation.

#### Why This Change Was Made

Previous attempt (#105727) added a regex-based detector with a pre-commit warning. ClawSweeper review identified three defects:

1. **Incomplete JSON5 line continuation handling** — regex only recognized LF/CR/CRLF, missing U+2028/U+2029
2. **Warning emitted before write commit** — rejected writes still alarmed users
3. **[P1] Uncovered `$include` writer** — `writeRootBoundJsonFile` (single-file `$include` path) also stripped comments silently

This fix:
- Replaces the regex with a **character-by-character lexical scanner** covering all JSON5 escape sequences including U+2028/U+2029
- Warning fires only from `logConfigOverwrite()` (post-`replaceFileAtomic`)
- `onCommitted` callback in `writeRootBoundJsonFile` extends coverage to included files
- Recovery guidance points to the pre-write `.bak` backup

#### User Impact

- Users with comments in `openclaw.json` or included files (`plugins.json5`, etc.) see a post-commit warning
- Warning tells users to diff against the pre-write backup to recover comments
- False positives eliminated: URLs, `//` in strings, all JSON5 line-continued strings correctly ignored
- Plain JSON configs produce no warning

#### Evidence

- **Type check:** `tsgo` passes with no errors
- **Tests:**
  - `io.parse.test.ts` — 11 tests (+9: lexical scanner)
  - `io.write-config.test.ts` — 103 tests (no regression)
  - `io.audit.test.ts` — all tests (no regression)
  - `mutate.test.ts` — 46 tests (+1: include-file comment-loss warning)
- **Change scope:** 4 files, +230 lines
  - `src/config/io.ts` — +68: `hasJSON5Comments()` scanner + warning in `logConfigOverwrite` (root writer)
  - `src/config/mutate.ts` — +18: `onCommitted` callback in `writeRootBoundJsonFile` (include writer)
  - `src/config/io.parse.test.ts` — +57: 9 focused scanner tests
  - `src/config/mutate.test.ts` — +85: 1 focused include-writer test
  - No new dependencies, no config/CLI/SDK/docs/changelog surface
- **Both write paths covered:**
  - Root writer (`replaceFileAtomic`): warning in `logConfigOverwrite` post-commit
  - Include writer (`writeRootBoundJsonFile`): warning via `onCommitted` callback
- **Real behavior proof** — actual `writeConfigFile` call against a JSON5-commented config on real filesystem:

```
====================================================================
  Config Write — JSON5 Comment-Loss Warning Proof
====================================================================

[setup] /tmp/oc-proof-8BLZLn/.openclaw/openclaw.json
[setup] 317 bytes, 3 line comments, 1 block comment

[read]  hash=422ddd0dd094 valid=true size=317
  ✓ config file found
  ✓ raw has // line comments
  ✓ raw has /* */ block comments
  ✓ raw has inline // comment

[write] mutating config (adding plugins.entries.demo)...
[write] file on disk (256 bytes):
        | {
        |   "gateway": {
        |     "mode": "local",
        |     "port": 18789
        |   },
        |   "meta": {
        |     "lastTouchedVersion": "2026.7.2",
        |     "lastTouchedAt": "2026-07-13T05:53:03.623Z"
        |   },
        |   "plugins": {
        |     "entries": {
        |       "demo": {
        |         "enabled": true
        |       }
        |     }

[check] comment-loss warning: PRESENT
[check]   Config write removed JSON5 comments from /tmp/oc-proof-8BLZLn/.openclaw/openclaw.json.
           A pre-write backup was saved to the config directory; diff it against the current
           file to recover commented-out settings.
  ✓ warning emitted after successful write
  ✓ warning names the config file
  ✓ warning tells user about backup
  ✓ written file is plain JSON (no //)

  ✓ new plugin entry persisted

[check] backup: /tmp/oc-proof-8BLZLn/.openclaw/openclaw.json.bak

The proof script:
1. Writes a real `openclaw.json` with `//` line comments, `/* */` block comments, and `// inline` comments
2. Calls `createConfigIO().writeConfigFile()` to mutate the config (adding a plugin entry)

target.title: fix(agents): tighten grepSchema context/limit from Type.Number to Type.Integer
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes #105822

**Problem**: `grepSchema.context` and `grepSchema.limit` use `Type.Number`, accepting fractional values like `1.5` or `10.5` that are semantically invalid for context lines and match counts.

**Solution**: Change both fields to `Type.Integer` so schema validation rejects floats before reaching tool logic, and export `grepSchema` so the unit test validates against the production schema rather than a reconstructed copy. Importing `grepSchema` from the grep module is safe for a unit test because the schema is a plain TypeBox object with no runtime side effects. This follows the same pattern applied to the `ls` tool schema in PR #105827.

**What changed**: In `src/agents/sessions/tools/grep.ts` — `Type.Number` → `Type.Integer` for `context` and `limit`, `const grepSchema` → `export const grepSchema`. Rewrote `grep.limit-schema.test.ts` to import and validate against the production schema (4 scenarios). Removed standalone `_validate_grep.mjs` (redundant).

**NOT changed**: Tool execution behavior, default values (context=0, limit=100), `normalizePositiveLimit` clamping, any other schema field, tool registration, or `grepSchema` visibility. Existing grep integration tests (`grep.stream-errors.test.ts`) continue to pass without any modification.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Schema-level rejection of float `context` and `limit` values via the exported production `grepSchema` — test imports the real schema, not a reconstructed copy.
**Real environment tested**: Linux x64, Node.js 25.9.0, OpenClaw `main@HEAD` with this patch applied.
**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: Direct validation of the exported `grepSchema` via `node --import tsx/esm -e "import { Check } from 'typebox/value'; import { grepSchema } from './src/agents/sessions/tools/grep.js'; ..."`
**After-fix evidence**: Test (1/1 passed) + terminal output (4/4 passed) — see below.
**Observed result after the fix**: `Check(grepSchema, { pattern: "foo", context: 1.5, limit: 50 })` = `false`; `Check(grepSchema, { pattern: "foo", context: 3, limit: 10.5 })` = `false`; `Check(grepSchema, { pattern: "foo", context: 3, limit: 50 })` = `true`; `Check(grepSchema, { pattern: "foo" })` = `true`.
**What was not tested**: End-to-end grep execution (covered by existing `grep.stream-errors.test.ts`).

## Tests and validation

```
$ pnpm test src/agents/sessions/tools/grep.limit-schema.test.ts --reporter=verbose

 ✓ |unit-fast| rejects float context and limit — validates against production grepSchema

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  1 passed (1)

$ node --import tsx/esm -e "..."

  PASS Check(grepSchema, {"pattern":"foo","context":3,"limit":50}) = true (expected true)
  PASS Check(grepSchema, {"pattern":"foo","context":1.5,"limit":50}) = false (expected false)
  PASS Check(grepSchema, {"pattern":"foo","context":3,"limit":10.5}) = false (expected false)
  PASS Check(grepSchema, {"pattern":"foo"}) = true (expected true)

4/4 passed (production schema validated)
```

Validated against the exported production `grepSchema`:

| Input | Expected | Result |
|-------|----------|--------|
| `{ pattern: "foo", context: 3, limit: 50 }` | ✅ accept | passed |
| `{ pattern: "foo", context: 1.5, limit: 50 }` | ❌ reject (float context) | passed |
| `{ pattern: "foo", context: 3, limit: 10.5 }` | ❌ reject (float limit) | passed |
| `{ pattern: "foo" }` (optionals omitted) | ✅ accept | passed |

The branch was rebased onto the latest upstream/main to resolve the stale-base issue flagged in the initial review.

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible — integers previously accepted by `Type.Number` remain accepted by `Type.Integer`
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations — production schema validated directly
- [ ] I have updated relevant documentation — schema is self-documenting via TypeBox types
- [x] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary

target.title: fix(gateway): add base64 validation before decode in talk-realtime-relay
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes #105846

**Problem**: Real-time relay audio frames use unpadded base64 encoding, but the `isValidBase64` guard from `chat-attachments.ts` requires length % 4 === 0, rejecting valid unpadded audio frames. This breaks relay clients sending standard unpadded base64.

**Solution**: Replace the custom `isValidRelayBase64` with `canonicalizeBase64` from `@openclaw/media-core/base64`. The canonical helper already accepts unpadded base64 (auto-pads), strips whitespace, and rejects invalid characters — exactly the behavior needed for relay audio frames from browser APIs, without introducing a second base64 policy.

**What changed**: In `src/gateway/talk-realtime-relay.ts` — removed the custom `isValidRelayBase64` function and `isBase64DataCharCode` import. Added `canonicalizeBase64` import from `@openclaw/media-core/base64`. Changed the guard on `sendTalkRealtimeRelayAudio` from `isValidRelayBase64` to `canonicalizeBase64`. No changes to `chat-attachments.ts` (the exports belong to PR #105837).

**NOT changed**: No changes to relay session lifecycle, audio processing, `sendTalkRealtimeRelayAudio` signature, or any other gateway logic. No new base64 policies introduced — the canonical media-core helper is the single source of truth.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Canonical base64 validation for real-time relay audio frames using `canonicalizeBase64` from `@openclaw/media-core/base64` — accepts unpadded base64, strips whitespace, rejects invalid input.
**Real environment tested**: Linux x64, Node.js 25.9.0, OpenClaw `main@HEAD` with this patch applied.
**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: `node --import tsx/esm -e "..."` (standalone validation against production `canonicalizeBase64`)
**After-fix evidence**: 5/5 validation scenarios passed with whitespace handling (see terminal output below).

target.title: fix(cli): use startsWith for loopback IPv4 check in container proxy
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`isLoopbackProxyHostname` used `split(".", 1)[0] === "127"` to detect 127.0.0.0/8 loopback addresses. While `isIP()` already rejects invalid octets (leading zeros, out-of-range) before this branch, `split(".", 1)[0]` is unnecessarily indirect and obscures the intent of matching the full 127.0.0.0/8 range.

## Why This Change Was Made

`startsWith("127.")` directly expresses the intent of matching any valid IPv4 address in the 127.0.0.0/8 loopback block. It is equivalent in behavior (since `isIP() === 4` already validated the format) but clearer and less fragile.

## User Impact

No behavior change — same loopback detection logic, just more readable and maintainable.

target.title: feat(skills): capture reusable techniques from successful work
target.body:
Closes #105672

## What Problem This Solves

Opt-in Skill Workshop autonomy can capture explicit corrections, but reusable procedures discovered during long successful work are otherwise lost when the user did not phrase the result as a correction.

## Why This Change Was Made

When autonomous capture is enabled, successful foreground turns with at least ten model iterations may schedule a separate learning review after the run has finished and the whole agent system has remained idle for 30 seconds. The delayed review rechecks live autonomy, sandbox, agent, provider, sender, and conversation tool policy before it starts.

The reviewer is isolated to the exact resolved provider and model, reuses the auth profile when available, and disables model fallback. It runs on a dedicated background lane and receives a bounded rendering of only the current turn. Its Skill Workshop surface permits list/inspect plus at most one create or revise mutation; live-skill updates and proposal lifecycle actions are unavailable. Every generated result remains a pending proposal for human review.

The evidence bar is intentionally narrow: concrete struggle, correction, repeated failure, or a stable procedure expected to save at least two future model/tool round trips. Routine success, one-off facts, preferences, transient failures, secrets, generic advice, and uncertain cases must abstain.

## User Impact

Users who explicitly enable autonomous Skill Workshop capture can receive reviewable learning proposals after meaningful work without delaying foreground requests. The feature remains off by default, waits for idle state across embedded and reply-backed runs, bounds retained work, serializes learning reviews, and never applies a proposal automatically.

The new Self-learning guide documents enablement, eligibility, transcript and provider behavior, cost and privacy implications, proposal-only permissions, review commands, and troubleshooting. Skill Workshop, skills configuration, navigation, and the generated docs map link to that guide.

## Evidence

- Blacksmith Testbox [run 29221332451](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29221332451): 32 focused scheduler, Workshop, and lane tests passed; Oxlint reported zero findings; `tsgo:core` and `tsgo:core:test` passed.

target.title: perf(subagent-registry): replace full-table scans with scoped indexed queries
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The `listSubagentRunsForController` hot path loads the **entire persisted subagent registry** (all rows from SQLite via `getSubagentRunsSnapshotForRead`) and performs synchronous `Array.filter()` scanning, blocking the event loop linearly with registry size. The SQLite schema already has `idx_subagent_runs_controller_session_key` but the store layer never uses it.

## What This PR Does

1. **Store layer** — Added `loadSubagentRunsForControllerFromSqlite`: a scoped Kysely query that uses the existing `idx_subagent_runs_controller_session_key` index with a compound predicate preserving the `controllerSessionKey || requesterSessionKey` fallback semantics. Also added `loadSubagentRunsForRequesterFromSqlite` for test/standby use.
2. **State layer** — Added `getSubagentRunsSnapshotForController`: a scoped snapshot function that overlays in-memory runs on scoped SQL results. **Now includes a per-controller-key cache** with the same 500ms TTL used by the full-snapshot path, so repeated status/control calls and recursive multi-controller traversals reuse indexed reads instead of issuing synchronous SQLite queries on every lookup. Cache entries are invalidated on `persistSubagentRunsToDisk`.
3. **Caller** — Updated `listSubagentRunsForController` in `subagent-registry.ts` and `subagent-registry-read.ts` to use the scoped snapshot. The `listSubagentRunsForRequester` path is **unchanged**.
4. **Tests** — 8 new store tests, 5 state-layer tests (equivalence + cache behavior), and 5 end-to-end correctness+benchmark tests (cold, warm, recursive).

No schema migration required — all needed indexes already exist.

## Evidence

### Benchmark results (10K records, ext4 SSD, Windows x64)

```
=== Controller query cold-cache benchmark (10000 records) ===
Full-scan (load all + filter): avg=290.75ms
Scoped   (indexed query):      avg=2.14ms
Cold-cache speedup: 136.1x

=== Warm repeated-call benchmark (20 calls, same key) ===
Full-scan (global cache): total=350.50ms avg=17.52ms
Scoped   (per-key cache): total=11.18ms avg=0.56ms
Warm speedup: 31.3x

=== Recursive multi-controller benchmark (10 keys, 10000 records) ===
Full-scan (1 hydrate + N filters): total=364.54ms avg=36.45ms
Scoped   (N indexed + cache):      total=99.03ms avg=9.90ms
Recursive speedup: 3.7x
```

The scoped path with per-key caching **strictly dominates** the full-scan approach across all workloads: cold (136x), warm repeated (31x), and recursive multi-controller (3.7x).

### Benchmark reproducer

```bash
pnpm vitest run src/agents/subagent-registry-scoped.bench.test.ts
```

### Correctness

- Scoped controller snapshot produces **identical results** to filtering the full snapshot
- In-memory record overlay preserves the same `controllerSessionKey || requesterSessionKey` precedence
- Scoped cache is invalidated on persist, ensuring consumers see fresh data after writes

### Tests

```bash
pnpm test src/agents/subagent-registry-state.test.ts
pnpm test src/agents/subagent-registry.store.sqlite.test.ts
pnpm test src/agents/subagent-registry.test.ts
pnpm test src/agents/subagent-registry-scoped.bench.test.ts
pnpm test src/agents/subagent-registry-read-context.test.ts
pnpm test src/auto-reply/reply/commands-subagents-status.test.ts
```

**268/268 passing, 0 failures, 0 regressions.**

### Files changed (8 files, +806/-5)

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `src/agents/subagent-registry.store.sqlite.ts` | +71: 2 scoped query functions |
| `src/agents/subagent-registry-state.ts` | +133: 2 scoped snapshot functions + per-key cache |

target.title: fix(tailscale): retry status json after serve startup
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes the transient `tailscale status --json` startup race in Tailscale Serve mode.

- retry only recognized daemon-readiness failures: local daemon connection errors and status probes terminated by the existing command timeout
- propagate missing binaries, permission failures, malformed JSON, and other permanent failures immediately
- retry the same detected Tailscale binary so fallback does not switch installations
- rebuild the branch from current `main` while preserving the latest Tailscale whois, Serve, and Funnel behavior

Closes #42798.

## Verification

- `node_modules/oxfmt/bin/oxfmt --check src/infra/tailscale.ts src/infra/tailscale.test.ts`
- `OPENCLAW_HEAVY_CHECK_LOCK_SCOPE=worktree node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/tailscale.test.ts src/gateway/server-tailscale.test.ts` (53 tests passed)
- `git diff --check`
- `node_modules/.bin/tsx /private/tmp/tailscale-91553-refresh-live-proof.ts` (3/3 real Serve cycles passed)
- final GitHub head `5a6e0cbc38b255c8b1acbdd916fceea10fb5fc17`: mergeable against current `main`, two changed files only

## Real behavior proof

Behavior addressed: Gateway Tailscale Serve startup now survives a transient first `tailscale status --json` daemon-readiness timeout and recovers the real tailnet hostname, while permanent command and parsing failures are not retried.

Real environment tested: Final PR head `5a6e0cbc38b255c8b1acbdd916fceea10fb5fc17` runtime surface on macOS arm64 with Homebrew Tailscale `1.98.8`, a real authorized `tailscaled` userspace daemon, real Tailscale Serve, and DNS name `openclaw-pr-91553-refresh.tail8ed022.ts.net`. The live-tested workspace and final PR head have byte-identical blobs for the changed runtime file (`6e6a1ee058c1ef5d7346572fe4818542e57f0600`), its test file (`aa32fb50679324d3782623f2e6467e2d1108e109`), the Gateway caller, and `runExec`.

Exact steps or command run after this patch: `node_modules/.bin/tsx /private/tmp/tailscale-91553-refresh-live-proof.ts`. The harness invoked the real `startGatewayTailscaleExposure({ tailscaleMode: "serve", port: 18789 })` path three times. In each cycle, the first real Homebrew `tailscale status --json` call used an unavailable daemon socket and hit the production 5-second `runExec` timeout; the retry used the authorized daemon socket, recovered the real DNS hostname, and then ran normal Serve cleanup.

Evidence after fix:
```json
{
  "environment": "macOS arm64 + Homebrew Tailscale 1.98.8 + real authorized tailscaled",
  "cycles": [
    {"cycle": 1, "firstStatusUsedUnavailableSocket": true, "statusAttempts": 2, "recoveredHostname": "openclaw-pr-91553-refresh.tail8ed022.ts.net", "serveEnabled": true, "cleanupCompleted": true},
    {"cycle": 2, "firstStatusUsedUnavailableSocket": true, "statusAttempts": 2, "recoveredHostname": "openclaw-pr-91553-refresh.tail8ed022.ts.net", "serveEnabled": true, "cleanupCompleted": true},
    {"cycle": 3, "firstStatusUsedUnavailableSocket": true, "statusAttempts": 2, "recoveredHostname": "openclaw-pr-91553-refresh.tail8ed022.ts.net", "serveEnabled": true, "cleanupCompleted": true}
  ]
}
```

Observed result after fix: All three real Serve cycles made exactly two status attempts, recovered the real tailnet DNS hostname after the first timeout, emitted no Serve warning, and completed cleanup. Focused tests additionally proved missing-binary and permission failures execute once and malformed JSON is not retried. The temporary proof node was logged out and its daemon stopped.

What was not tested: The Homebrew daemon ran in official userspace-networking mode rather than as a root launchd system daemon. The startup race was deterministically induced through an unavailable socket and the real production timeout rather than waiting for nondeterministic host load. Funnel mode and unrelated Gateway paths were not exercised.
